title: Uniform length bound for controlled bad exponent sequences
statement: For every integer $r\geq0$ and every function $h:\mathbf N\to\mathbf N$, there is $L=L(r,h)\in\mathbf N$ such that the following holds. If $n\in\mathbf N$ and $\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{n-1}\in\mathbf N^r$ satisfy $\sum_{a=1}^r\alpha_{i,a}\leq h(i)$ for every $i<n$, and for every $i<j<n$ there is a coordinate $a$ with $\alpha_{i,a}>\alpha_{j,a}$, then $n\leq L$. Thus no earlier tuple is coordinatewise at most any later tuple. The cases $r=0$, $n=0$, and functions $h$ taking the value zero are included; no monotonicity of $h$ is required. Here finite index sets have the meaning of [def-sfb-finite-infinite-set]; the sequence is indexed by the finite set $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$.

source.place: Theorem 8.2, printed p.773, is the surrounding uniform-bound result, not this combinatorial lemma. Agent-supplied controlled-Dickson argument for an alternative existence-only proof; local PDF WANTED; no Stacks tag asserted.

proof.text: Fix $r,h$. Let $E_m$ be the set of tuples $(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})$ satisfying the two conditions in the statement. Each coordinate of $\alpha_i$ lies in $\{0,\ldots,h(i)\}$, since it is nonnegative and at most the coordinate sum. Thus $E_m$ embeds into the product, over $i<m$ and $a=1,\ldots,r$, of these finite intervals, and has at most $\prod_{i<m}(h(i)+1)^r$ elements. This proves finiteness in the sense of [def-sfb-finite-infinite-set]; it does not require $h$ to be monotone. $E_0$ consists of the empty tuple.

proof.text: Suppose, for contradiction, that the possible lengths have no bound. For every $m$ choose a permitted sequence of length $n>m$ and restrict it to its first $m$ terms; this shows $E_m\ne\varnothing$. For $m\leq n$, restriction to the first $m$ terms maps $E_n$ to $E_m$: all retained inequalities have the same indices and the same bounds $h(i)$. Restriction to the same length is the identity, and restricting twice equals restricting once. Consequently the $E_m$ form a functor from the small category $\mathbf N^{\mathrm{op}}$ to sets. This category is cofiltered: it is nonempty, $\max(m,n)$ maps to $m,n$, and parallel arrows are equal.

source.place: Tag 086J, lemma-nonempty-limit; agent controlled-prefix application, combined with Mathlib/Order/WellQuasiOrder.lean, Pi.wellQuasiOrderedLE, lines 215--217.

proof.text: Apply [lem-trf-cofiltered-finite-sets-section] to this diagram: its index category is small and cofiltered by Step 2, and its values are finite and nonempty by Steps 1--2. Obtain $s_m\in E_m$ with every prefix restriction of $s_n$ equal to $s_m$ for $m\leq n$. Define $\beta_i$ to be entry $i$ of $s_{i+1}$. If $m>i$, compatibility with $s_{i+1}$ shows that entry $i$ of $s_m$ is $\beta_i$. In particular, for $i<j$, both $\beta_i,\beta_j$ are the corresponding entries of $s_{j+1}$, so $\beta_i\not\leq\beta_j$ coordinatewise. No surjectivity of restriction maps is assumed.

source.place: Tag 086J, lemma-nonempty-limit; agent controlled-prefix application, combined with Mathlib/Order/WellQuasiOrder.lean, Pi.wellQuasiOrderedLE, lines 215--217.

proof.text: By [lem-trf-dickson-exponent-sequences], the sequence $(\beta_i)_{i\in\mathbf N}$ in $\mathbf N^r$ has $i<j$ with $\beta_i\leq\beta_j$, contradicting Step 3. Hence the lengths are bounded; choose such a natural-number bound as $L(r,h)$. The construction involved only $r,h$. For $r=0$ there is only one empty exponent tuple, and two terms cannot satisfy the required strict-coordinate condition, so $L=1$ works. If $h(0)=0$, the first tuple must be zero, and again length at most one is possible; zeros at later indices cause no difficulty in the same proof. The empty sequence always satisfies the conditions and $0\leq L$.
